title: How to Start a Toy Rotation Before the Holidays (So the Playroom Stays Playable)
description: A simple toy rotation system for busy parents: fewer toys out, less cleanup, more play. Easy setup steps plus 7 Amazon finds for toy storage.
intro:
If your kids have a mountain of toys and still say "I'm bored," you're not alone. Too many toys out at once can make it hard for kids (and us) to choose anything. Everything gets dumped, nothing gets played with, and cleanup takes an hour.

Toy rotation is a simple fix. You keep only some of the toys out and store the rest. Every week or two, you swap. Old toys feel new again, and the playroom has a fighting chance of getting cleaned up.

Before the holidays is the perfect time to start, because new toys are coming and you want somewhere for them to go. Here's an easy setup, plus seven Amazon finds that make rotating quick.

sections.heading: Why rotation works for busy brains (big and small)
sections.body:
Fewer toys out means fewer things to put away. That's the whole magic. When a kid can see eight choices instead of eighty, cleanup at the end of the day is a five-minute job instead of a battle.

It's easier for us, too. Rotation gives you a reason to look at toys regularly, so broken ones and outgrown ones leave the house before they pile up.

sections.heading: Step 1: Sort into big, loose groups
sections.body:
Set a timer for 15 minutes and pull toys into rough piles: building, pretend play, cars, art, puzzles and games, stuffed animals, books. Don't be precise. "Roughly the same kind of toy" is good enough.

If 15 minutes isn't enough to get through everything, stop anyway and finish another day. A half-sorted toy room is still progress.

sections.heading: Step 2: Fill your rotation bins
sections.body:
Get four to six bins with lids. Into each bin, put a little from each group: a few building toys, one puzzle, a couple of cars, some pretend play. Each bin should feel like a mini toy room on its own.

Label the bins with a number (Bin 1, Bin 2) so you know which one comes out next. Clear bins make it easy to see what's in each one.

sections.heading: Step 3: Pick a storage spot out of sight
sections.body:
The bins that aren't in use go somewhere kids can't easily reach: a closet shelf, under a bed, the garage or the basement. Out of sight is important. If kids can see them, they'll want everything at once.

Keep favorite comfort toys and books out all the time. Rotation is for the extras, not the stuffed bunny they sleep with.

sections.heading: Step 4: Swap on a schedule (loosely)
sections.body:
Pick a swap rhythm: every Sunday, every other week, or whenever the kids seem bored. Set a phone reminder so the swap actually happens.

When you swap, put the current toys back in their bin, put the bin away and bring out the next number. It takes about 10 minutes. Kids often love helping with "new toy day."

sections.heading: Step 5: Make room for holiday gifts
sections.body:
When new toys arrive, don't put them all out at once. Pick a few to play with right away and tuck the rest into rotation bins. That stretches the excitement out for months instead of one overwhelmed afternoon.

If the bins are getting too full, that's your cue to donate a few older toys before adding new ones.

outro:
Toy rotation isn't about having fewer toys forever. It's about having fewer toys *out*, so play feels fresh and cleanup feels possible. Start with whatever bins you already own and upgrade later.
